transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-20
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 56 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Reyes (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (CascadeGuard CTO), Elena Morales (SRE Lead), Samir Khan (Dir Eng), Jia Li (Compliance), Omar Rizvi (Prod Eng)

Summary:
Brief follow-up after last night's service degradation; focus on straight-line mitigations, handoff to ops, and compliance sign-off for longer-term Dedicated pilot. Aim is to leave with clear owners and a dry-run plan.

Topics:
1) What tripped during the window (KV-cache eviction storm + batching throttle).
2) Immediate mitigations (circuit-breaker, fallback model variant, prefix cache warming).
3) Runbook and canary plan for Dedicated pilot.
4) Data residency and audit log questions from compliance.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: okay, hi everyone, thanks for joining on short notice, um we'll do kind of a tight ninety minute — sorry — a tight 45/60 minute sync. Quick intros if we need them, but assume folks saw the postmortem draft.
[00:23] Raj: yeah thanks Maya I skimmed, appreciate the quick turnaround. Biggest thing for us is the customer-facing error rate spike at 02:14 UTC, that was — we had pages.
[00:34] Elena: yes, it looked like the KV cache had a cascading eviction and then the continuous batching started to pile on and latency climbed and our downstream timeouts kicked in.
[00:47] Liam: right, from Redwood side, what we saw in the traces is a rapid increase in long-tail sequences that caused the per-shard queue to exceed the batching window. We also had a compaction job overlap which amplified IO to the model store, so two compounding factors.
[01:08] Samir: can you clarify compaction job? is that on our side or Redwood infra?
[01:15] Liam: it was an internal housekeeping process on the Dedicated routing layer — sorry, on the shared caching tier — that we triggered for cleanup; timing misaligned with your heavy traffic pattern. We did roll back the compaction mid-incident.
[01:36] Raj: ok, we need that separated in the runbook, who owns what, because we don't want cross-domain ops touching the same cache window during peak.
[01:45] Maya: agreed. high level mitigations we propose: immediate circuit-breaker at the route layer to fail fast on elevated queue depth; fallback to a smaller, quantized model variant for non-critical requests; and prefix/KV cache warming for expected hot keys during peak.
[02:10] Elena: circuit-breaker is fine, but we need a safe fallback path and a clear way to route only particular traffic — i.e. authenticated contracts get stricter SLOs.
[02:25] Jia: from compliance: audit logs for any fallback decisions — we need immutable audit records, timestamps, and KMS-backed encryption for the logs. Also SOC2 artifacts for the Dedicated pilot.
[02:42] Maya: yes we'll include an audit appendix. Redwood supports KMS integration and we can provide the encryption architecture diagram and the SOC2 summary as part of the security pack.
[02:58] Omar: one thing I noticed: during the incident auto-scaling didn't spin up fast enough for the batch worker pool, maybe due to the scaling policy's sampling window. Can we recommend an aggressive scale policy for pilot?
[03:16] Liam: absolutely, for pilot we suggest a shorter evaluation window and explicit warm pools with pre-warmed GPUs on Dedicated so we avoid cold-start throttles. Also recommend the burst capacity knob for sub-minute surges.
[03:36] Raj: cost is a concern, so we don't want to pay for permanently warm pools. We want predictable spend — how do you balance cost vs resilience?
[03:48] Maya: two-tier approach: 1) Short-term: enable targeted warm pools for specific routes during high-risk windows (business hours, launches). 2) Mid-term: run a 2-week Dedicated pilot limited to 25% of traffic for heavy inference paths to quantify unit cost vs error reduction. We'll provide modeling.
[04:15] Samir: and what's the rollback plan if Dedicated pilot introduces issues? we need canary switches and auto-failback to hosted models.
[04:26] Liam: we have automated rollbacks — traffic can be gradually shifted and we keep sticky sessions pinned to previous variants until cutover completes. We'll add explicit abort triggers in the canary policy.
[04:45] Elena: re: the KV cache eviction — can we get the exact TTLs, eviction policy and which keys lost hotness? That will help us simulate.
[04:55] Liam: yes, I'll export the cache metrics and the eviction trace. There's a known issue with the cache compaction heuristics when hot-key churn is high; we have a config patch that switches to frequency-based eviction rather than age-only. That helped in internal repro.
[05:22] Raj: who owns running the repro? CascadeGuard or Redwood?
[05:28] Maya: joint. Redwood will provide a traffic pattern generator and a test harness; CascadeGuard will run it in a staging env and share traces. We'll coordinate timing.
[05:40] Jia: a compliance question — for the pilot where logs are pushed to a shared bucket, can we ensure access controls and retention meet our policy? we need 12 months retention and RBAC.
[05:53] Maya: yes we can configure S3 lifecycle and bucket policies; we'll include sample IAM roles in the security appendix.
[06:07] Omar: during the incident our monitoring alarms were noisy and we couldn't differentiate true positive rate. Can we add a severity-tiered alerting based on token-latency percentile thresholds?
[06:21] Liam: yes, propose two new alerts: p95 latency crossing threshold for service degradation and a separate queue-depth alarm that triggers when combined with p99 latency — that reduces noisy ones. We'll provide a recommended threshold set.
[06:40] Raj: timeline — we need first mitigation (circuit-breaker + fallback) in place before the next expected release on 2026-11-29. Can you commit?
[06:52] Maya: yes, short-term mitigations are doable; we'll ship configuration and runbook by 2026-11-24.
[07:01] Samir: great. one more: will Redwood's SDK changes be needed for our clients to opt into degraded-mode responses? or is it transparent?
[07:12] Liam: transparent at the API layer — degraded responses are flagged in headers and body metadata so clients can choose to retry or degrade. We'll document header names and error codes.
[07:30] Raj: ok let's recap next steps and owners.
[07:36] Maya: recap — Maya to send mitigations + security appendix; Liam to export cache traces and batching config; Elena/Omar to run repro and share traces; Raj to approve pilot budget; all to attend a runbook dry-run next week.
[07:58] Elena: can we set the dry-run for the 30th morning? we have on-call coverage then.
[08:05] Maya: yes I'll propose two slots, 09:00 and 15:00 PST, and collect votes.
[08:15] Jia: please include the compliance checklist in the docs so we can sign off quickly.
[08:22] Maya: noted. anything else?
[08:28] Raj: no, thanks everyone. appreciate the quick response.
[08:33] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up with materials and calendar invite.

End of transcript.

Notes: transcription includes a few mis-attributed words (compaction/process names approximate). Some proper nouns may be slightly off in auto-transcript. Action items enumerated above and in metadata.
